q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way in which cultural developments contributed to German nationalism in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the revolutions of 1848 failed to achieve German unification, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which Bismarck's approach to unification differed from the approach of the 1848 revolutionaries.

sample_answers.a: Writers, composers, and scholars promoted a shared German language, folklore, and history — through works like the Grimm brothers' fairy tales — giving Germans who lived under dozens of separate states a sense of common cultural identity.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, the 1848 revolutionaries relied on parliamentary debate and moral persuasion but lacked military power; when the Frankfurt Parliament offered the German crown to the Prussian king, he refused it from a popular assembly, and the movement collapsed without an army to enforce its decisions.
sample_answers.c: Where the 1848 revolutionaries sought unification through liberal constitutions and elected parliaments, Bismarck pursued it through Prussian military strength and calculated wars against Denmark, Austria, and France, uniting Germany 'from above' under Prussian dominance rather than through popular sovereignty.

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain the rise of German nationalism as a process in which cultural identity preceded political unity. Long before Germany existed as a state, writers, linguists, and composers cultivated the idea of a German nation defined by shared language and heritage, giving people scattered across dozens of principalities a sense of belonging to something larger. The revolutions of 1848 briefly raised the hope that this cultural nation could become a political one through liberal parliaments, but the Frankfurt Parliament's failure — it debated constitutions while possessing no army and no treasury — demonstrated the limits of unification by persuasion alone. German unity was ultimately achieved not by the liberals of 1848 but by Otto von Bismarck, who harnessed Prussian military power and waged a series of calculated wars that forced the German states together under Prussian leadership.
—Historian's account of German nationalism in the period c. 1750–1900

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Bismarck makes about how the great questions of the day will be settled.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Bismarck's policies between 1864 and 1871 put this claim into practice.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Bismarck's 'iron and blood' approach succeeded where the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 had failed.

sample_answers.a: Bismarck claims that the great questions of the time will be settled not by speeches and majority votes — the methods of 1848 — but by 'iron and blood,' meaning military force and war.
sample_answers.b: Bismarck led Prussia into three wars — against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866), and France (1870–71) — each victory bringing more German states under Prussian leadership and culminating in the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles.
sample_answers.c: Bismarck commanded the Prussian state and its powerful army, so he could impose unification by force and diplomacy; the Frankfurt Parliament had only moral authority and no troops or revenue, so its decisions could be ignored by the very princes it sought to unite.

q2.stimulus:
The great questions of the time will not be resolved by speeches and majority decisions — that was the great mistake of 1848 and 1849 — but by iron and blood.
—Otto von Bismarck, speech to the Prussian parliament, 1862

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the painting that connects it to German nationalist aspirations in 1848.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the painting reflects the liberal goals of the Frankfurt Parliament.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why the vision of German unity shown in the painting was not achieved in 1848.

sample_answers.a: The female figure of Germania wears the oak-leaf crown and holds symbols of German unity, personifying the hope that the many German states could become one nation — the central aspiration of the 1848 nationalists.
sample_answers.b: The painting was created for St. Paul's Church in Frankfurt, where the elected Frankfurt Parliament met; its imagery of a unified, free Germany reflects the parliament's liberal goals of constitutional government, civil rights, and national unity achieved through representative institutions.
sample_answers.c: The Frankfurt Parliament had no army, no treasury, and no means to compel the German princes; when it offered the imperial crown to the King of Prussia, he rejected a crown 'from the gutter' of popular revolution, and the princes suppressed the movement by force.

q3.stimulus: The image is Philipp Veit's 1848 painting Germania, created for St. Paul's Church in Frankfurt am Main, where the Frankfurt Parliament — Germany's first freely elected national assembly — was meeting during the revolutions of 1848. The painting shows Germania, the female personification of the German nation, adorned with symbols of German unity and freedom. It became an iconic image of the liberal nationalist hopes of 1848.
